card.name: Son de los Diablos
card.tagline: An Afro-Peruvian devil dance of Lima streets, featuring zapateo and the rattle of jawbones.
card.profile: Son de los Diablos is an energetic Afro-Peruvian street dance originating in Lima and Cañete. Developed during the Viceroyalty of Peru, it blends African, Spanish, and Amerindian influences into a vibrant carnival tradition. Performers don devil masks, tails, and tridents while marching in cuadrillas led by a caporal. Accompanied by guitars, the wooden cajita, and the quijada de burro, dancers terrify passersby with acrobatic leaps and zapateo footwork.
card.insight: Banned by the Catholic Church in 1817 and disappearing mid-20th century, this devil comparsa was dramatically revived from 19th-century watercolors by Pancho Fierro.
card.profile_long:
The Son de los Diablos is an Afro-Peruvian dance that developed as a mixture of African, Spanish, and Amerindian rhythms during the Viceroyalty of Peru. According to researcher Nicomedes Santa Cruz, despite popular opinion, the dance has no direct links with African rituals or the Andean Morenada, though it bears a very slight similarity to the Diabladas of Oruro in Bolivia. Developed in the Spanish colony and assimilated by black slaves, the tradition evolved dynamically in the urban landscape of Lima.

Following the independence of Peru in 1821, people of African descent lived predominantly in alleyways near the churches and plazas of Lima, where public festivities took place. Before major celebrations, these communities formed gangs known as cuadrillas to perform the Son de los Diablos. Much like the broader Diablada tradition, the dance was heavily influenced by Spanish Corpus Christi celebrations. Initially accompanying Corpus Christi processions, it eventually transitioned into a core feature of the local Carnival festivities.

The historical trajectory of the dance saw intense institutional friction. It was famously banned from religious celebrations by the Catholic Church in 1817. Nonetheless, it remained an integral part of Lima's carnival celebrations until the early 20th century, with records also placing its practice during the San Juan festivals in the hacienda Arona de San Luis de Cañete during the 1930s. The dance eventually vanished from Lima's streets by the mid-20th century, compounded by the official prohibition of carnival play in 1958 and the suspension of holiday periods following Carnival Sunday.

Despite its decline in public spaces, the tradition was preserved through the historical record, most notably the 19th-century watercolors of artist Pancho Fierro, which vividly captured how the dance was performed. A major turning point occurred in 1956 when the group Estampas de Pancho Fierro recreated the dance for stage presentations. Later, in 1986, the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo rescued the cultural tradition, successfully returning the dance back to the streets of Lima.

Choreographically, the dance portrays the devil using elaborate masks, tails, and tridents. Dancers parade through the streets as a comparsa under the command of a leader known as the caporal. The movement vocabulary includes intricate pasadas de zapateo (foot-tapping sequences), acrobatic feats, and theatrical shouts designed to frighten onlookers. 

Musically, the dance is anchored by distinct percussion instruments. A distinguishing factor of the Son de los Diablos is its use of the cajita—a small wooden box that opens and closes to create a crisp, dry percussion sound—and the quijada, the dried jawbone of a horse, donkey, or mule that produces a raspy buzz when struck or scraped. These are traditionally complemented by guitars and vocal accompaniment, driving the rhythmic momentum of the street procession.

card.sacred_note: While initially tied to Catholic Corpus Christi celebrations before being banned by the Church in 1817, the dance functions primarily as a secular carnival and theatrical performance tradition rather than a restricted sacred ritual.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed during the Viceroyalty of Peru with roots in the Iberian Peninsula, the dance was assimilated by enslaved and free Africans. Post-independence (1821), communities in Lima's alleyways formed cuadrillas to perform it during Corpus Christi and later Carnival. Banned by the Church in 1817 and fading mid-20th century, it was revived on stage in 1956 by Estampas de Pancho Fierro and returned to the streets in 1986 by the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced as a street comparsa led by a caporal. The choreography features dynamic pasadas de zapateo, acrobatic movements, and startling shouts to engage or frighten passersby.
sections.music_and_instruments: Driven by guitars, the cajita (a small wooden box opened and closed for rhythmic accents), and the quijada de burro (a donkey, horse, or mule jawbone hit to create a raspy buzz).
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers dress as devils, wearing horned masks, tails, and holding tridents, as depicted in 19th-century watercolors by Pancho Fierro. Set primarily in public streets, plazas, and alleys during carnivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally associated with Corpus Christi and subsequently with Carnival and regional festival dates like San Juan in Cañete. It serves as an expression of Afro-Peruvian identity, reclaiming public space through theatricality.
sections.notable_figures: Nicomedes Santa Cruz (researcher), Pancho Fierro (19th-century watercolorist), José Durand (revivalist in the 1950s), and the Movimiento Negro Francisco Congo (returned the dance to the streets in 1986).
sections.regional_variants: Practiced historically and currently in Lima and the Cañete Province (such as San Luis de Cañete), sharing thematic traits with the broader Andean Diablada tradition while retaining distinct Afro-Peruvian instrumentation.
sections.lineage: Evolved from Spanish colonial and Catholic celebrations combined with Afro-Peruvian performance practices, drawing slight comparative parallels to the Diabladas of Oruro.
